n: Two angels arrive in Sodom at evening. Lot is sitting in the city gate, where leaders and elders met—suggesting he has become a respected resident. Like Abraham, he warmly greets the strangers.

f.g: The city gate was the center of public business, legal decisions, and leadership.

n: Lot urges them to stay at his house. The angels say they will spend the night in the town square, perhaps testing Lot or the city.

f.g: Spend the night in the open square.

n: Lot insists—he knows the streets are dangerous—and serves them a meal with unleavened bread, which could be made quickly.

f.g: Bread made without yeast, quick to prepare; later associated with the Passover deliverance.

n: Before bedtime the entire male population surrounds the house—young and old, from every part of town. The city’s corruption is complete.
The mob demands the visitors so they may “know” them—meaning to sexually assault them. Violent abuse of guests violated the sacred duty of hospitality.

f.g: A Hebrew idiom for sexual relations; here it means rape.

n: Lot bravely steps outside and shuts the door behind him to protect his guests.

f.g: Lot puts himself between the mob and his guests.

n: Lot begs the men not to commit such evil, calling them “brethren” in hopes of reasoning with them.

In KJV Genesis, Lot desperately offers his daughters instead—a shocking offer that shows how deeply Sodom had warped even Lot. The Joseph Smith Translation changes this so that Lot refuses to give up his daughters.

f.g: JST Genesis 19:9-15 revises this passage: the mob seeks the daughters and Lot refuses to hand them over.

f.w: under the shadow of my roof

n: The mob turns on Lot, mocking him as a foreigner trying to judge them. They rush forward to break down the door.

f.w: he will needs be a judge
f.g: “He wants to play the judge over us!”

n: The angels pull Lot inside and shut the door—the guests now protect their host.
The angels strike the men with blindness, so they grope in vain for the door. Their spiritual blindness becomes physical.

f.g: A rare Hebrew word suggesting a sudden dazzling or confusion of sight (compare 2 Kings 6:18).

n: The angels urge Lot to gather all his family and get them out of the city.

f.g: Do you have any other family members here?

n: They reveal their mission: the Lord has sent them to destroy the city because of the great outcry against it.
Lot warns his sons-in-law, but they think he is joking. When people are steeped in the world, warnings of danger can sound ridiculous.
At dawn the angels urge Lot to hurry with his wife and daughters before they are swept away.
Lot hesitates, perhaps attached to his home and possessions. The angels take the family by the hand and lead them out. The text notes this is because the Lord was merciful.

f.w: the LORD being merciful unto him

n: They are told to flee to the hills without looking back or stopping. Escaping evil requires leaving it completely behind.
Lot protests, still reluctant.
Lot thanks God for saving him but fears he cannot reach the mountains safely.
Lot asks to flee to a nearby small town instead. He keeps pointing out how small it is, as if a small city must hold only small sins.

f.w: is it not a little one?
f.g: Wordplay: Hebrew mitsʿar, “a little thing,” sounds like Zoar.

n: The angel grants Lot’s request and spares that town for his sake.
The angel urges haste; the destruction must wait until Lot is safe. The town is named Zoar, meaning “small.”
The sun has risen by the time Lot reaches Zoar.
The Lord rains burning sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah. Some suggest an earthquake ignited the region’s tar and gas deposits, but the text stresses that the judgment came from God.

f.g: Sulfur, which burns with intense heat and a suffocating smell.

f.w: fire from the LORD out of heaven

n: The cities, the whole plain, its people, and even its plants are destroyed. Sodom becomes a lasting symbol of judgment for wickedness.
Lot’s wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt. Jesus later said, “Remember Lot’s wife”—a warning against longing for a sinful past.

f.g: The Dead Sea region is still known for its salt formations.

n: Early the next morning Abraham returns to the place where he had pleaded with the Lord.

f.w: where he stood before the LORD

n: He sees smoke rising from the plain like smoke from a furnace. Not even ten righteous people were found.
God “remembered Abraham” and rescued Lot. Lot was saved largely because of Abraham’s intercession and covenant relationship with God.
Lot, now afraid to stay in Zoar, moves to the hills—where the angels first told him to go—and lives in a cave with his daughters. He has lost nearly everything.

f.g: A sad end for a man who once had flocks, herds, and a house in the city.

n: Lot’s older daughter fears they will never have husbands or children. They may have thought the destruction had been worldwide.

f.w: there is not a man in the earth
f.g: Perhaps they believed no men remained, or none would marry into their family.

n: The daughters plan to get their father drunk and have children by him. Their desperate plan shows the lasting influence of Sodom’s values.

f.g: To keep their father’s family line alive.

n: The older daughter carries out the plan while Lot is too drunk to know what is happening.
The next day she urges her younger sister to do the same.
The younger daughter follows the same plan. The account is told plainly and without approval.

f.g: The second night, repeating the wrong.

n: Both daughters become pregnant by their father.
The older daughter’s son, Moab, becomes the ancestor of the Moabites, Israel’s neighbors east of the Dead Sea. Ruth, an ancestor of David and Jesus, was a Moabite.
The younger daughter’s son, Ben-ammi, becomes the ancestor of the Ammonites, another neighboring people east of the Jordan.
